articles.title: Região de Campinas: 1 a cada 4 veículos tem licenciamento vencimento | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento do Detran-SP aponta 617.857 documentos atrasados até setembro; infração gravíssima pode resultar em multa, pontos na CNH e remoção do veículo.
articles.summary: Levantamento do Detran-SP aponta 617.857 documentos atrasados até setembro; infração gravíssima pode resultar em multa, pontos na CNH e remoção do veículo.
articles.body:
Imagem de arquivo mostra carros trafegando em via de Campinas (SP). — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

Cerca de um em cada quatro veículos da região de Campinas está com o licenciamento vencido, em média, segundo levantamento do Departamento Estadual de Trânsito de São Paulo (Detran-SP).

Os dados mostram que 617.857 veículos estavam com o documento em atraso até setembro deste ano, em uma frota ativa de 2.608.986 veículos. Na prática, os licenciamentos vencidos representam 23,7% da frota da região.

O número de licenciamentos vencidos registrado em nove meses em 2026 é o maior dos últimos cinco anos na série disponibilizada pelo Detran-SP. Ao mesmo tempo, a frota ativa da região cresceu de 2.364.035 veículos em 2022 para 2.608.986 em 2026, aumento de quase 245 mil veículos no período.

Licenciamentos na região de Campinas até setembro

O levantamento considera os licenciamentos de carros, motos e outros veículos com vencimento até setembro. Os dados de outubro, novembro e dezembro ficaram de fora porque, neste ano, os prazos ainda não venceram.

Os números podem incluir licenciamentos residuais de anos anteriores que continuam pendentes de pagamento, segundo o Detran-SP.

Circular com o licenciamento vencido é uma infração gravíssima, de acordo com o artigo 230 do Código de Trânsito Brasileiro (CTB).

A penalidade prevê multa de R$ 293,47, sete pontos na Carteira Nacional de Habilitação (CNH) e risco de remoção do veículo para o pátio.

Além da multa, o proprietário pode ter despesas adicionais com guincho, diárias de estadia no pátio, taxa de liberação do veículo e quitação dos débitos pendentes, como o próprio licenciamento, IPVA e eventuais multas.

Carros; veículos; trânsito em via de Campinas. — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

Segundo o Detran-SP, a forma mais rápida de fazer o licenciamento é pelo portal do órgão.

Para concluir o procedimento, o proprietário deve quitar eventuais multas de trânsito e o IPVA, informar o número do Renavam e pagar a taxa de licenciamento, atualmente de R$ 174,08.

Após o pagamento, o Certificado de Registro e Licenciamento de Veículo em meio digital (CRLV-e) pode ser baixado pelos portais do Detran-SP, do Poupatempo e da Secretaria Nacional de Trânsito (Senatran), além dos aplicativos Detran-SP, Poupatempo Digital e CNH do Brasil.

O documento pode ser armazenado no celular ou impresso em papel comum. Segundo o Detran-SP, neste ano a atualização ocorre de forma instantânea após a compensação do pagamento.

O pagamento também pode ser feito por internet banking, aplicativos bancários, caixas eletrônicos e bancos conveniados.

Caso o licenciamento não apareça disponível para quitação, o proprietário deve verificar a existência de pendências, como multas, débitos tributários ou bloqueios administrativos e judiciais.

articles.title: Two old-school Japanese mobile games are shutting down over the PHP exploit.
articles.summary:
World Quest and Save My Demonic World have run for over a decade, but they’re built on older tech that the developers say can’t be updated to patch the apocalyptic PHP exploit disclosed this week. Because the vulnerability affects almost 20 years of PHP, big chunks of internet history are in danger of being lost. Per Kotaku:
> Many old websites and services that are no longer being actively updated (or may simply be too old to receive the update, as was the case for these two games) are now at risk of permanently going offline. Such an event would lock swathes of the old internet from public view, including bits that were already beginning to break down and become inaccessible.

articles.title: US weekly jobless claims near 57-year lows, underscore labor market stability
articles.summary: By Lucia Mutikani WASHINGTON, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits dropped to near 57-year lows last week a...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits dropped to near 57-year lows last week amid low layoffs, suggesting a modest pickup in job growth in October after September's underwhelming performance.

The weekly jobless claims report from the Labor Department on Thursday, the most timely data on the economy's health, ‌continued to show no material stress in the labor market from the oil price shock stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Economists say strong growth in profits amid robust domestic demand, ‌and a smaller workforce against the backdrop of retirements and an immigration crackdown by the Trump administration, were shielding workers from layoffs.

There are, however, worries that tightening financial conditions and higher interest rates because of the drawn-out Middle East conflict could undercut ​the labor market next year.

"The administration's immigration policies may have tightened up the labor markets where companies are unable to find the help they need to produce their goods and services so they are holding tight to the workers they have," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "Workers are suddenly irreplaceable in many industries."

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits fell 6,000 to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended October 17. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 200,000 claims for the latest week. It was the sixth consecutive week that claims remained at or below the 200,000 mark. Claims are within striking distance of the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, ‌which was the lowest reading since 1969.

The claims data covered the period ⁠during which the government surveyed business establishments for the nonfarm payrolls component of October's employment report. The four-week moving average of claims, seen as a better measure of labor market trends as it irons out week-to-week volatility, fell between the September and October survey weeks.

At face value that would suggest an improvement in payroll ⁠gains this month. Payrolls increased by 29,000 jobs in September after rebounding by 133,000 in August. Payrolls tend to underperform when Labor Day falls relatively late in the month as was the case in September. Economists continue to view the labor market as still in a "low-hire, low-fire" state.

But uncertainty from the war and tariffs on imports has stymied hiring. Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower. The dollar was little changed against a basket of currencies. US ​Treasury ​yields fell.

articles.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia had record lobbying quarters
articles.summary: Leading AI companies are ramping up their federal lobbying spending, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia having their biggest lobbying quarters yet ahead of the midterms.
articles.body: It was a busy summer for AI lobbyists. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nvidia each had their highest-spending lobbying quarter between July and September, federal disclosures show. Nvidia spent the most of the group at $2.2 million, followed by Anthropic’s $2.1 million and OpenAI’s $1.5 million. Compared to other Big Tech companies with long-established presences in Washington, the sums aren’t out of the ordinary. Microsoft, for example, has spent at least $2 million a quarter going back to 2021, and Google regularly spends over $3 million, including this quarter. But it’s a clear signal that the three AI firms recognize how important shaping policy has become. Tech CEOs were already visible fixtures in Washington during this period, with many of them attending a White House lunch with President Donald Trump in late September, which resulted in a “morally binding” AI safety accord that they agreed to. The lobbying disclosures show that even more discussions were happening frequently behind the scenes, during a time just before Trump named his AI czar and task force. With Democrats expected to win back at least some control in Congress after this year’s midterm elections, AI companies may only find it more important to engage with lawmakers who see cracking down on the industry as a winning issue. Anthropic included a detailed list of bills, executive orders, and other topics it lobbied Congress and the White House about in the third quarter. Among them were AI-related provisions in the Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA), export control provisions in the AI Overwatch Act, Trump’s executive order renaming AI “Super Intelligence,” and the Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to put energy costs for data centers on their developers. OpenAI’s lobbying looks like a response to some of the fallout from the Hugging Face attack, though the disclosures only list high-level topics. In addition to engaging on issues like copyright, OpenAI lobbied Congress, the White House, the Small Business Administration, and the Commerce and State Departments over cybersecurity evaluations for frontier models, AI safety oversight frameworks, and antitrust protections for information sharing. Nvidia lobbied Congress, as well as several different federal agencies and White House offices, on issues including 6G networks, “responsible AI design,” competition policy, quantum computing, and export control policy. Apple also had a record-breaking quarter, spending $3.1 million and engaging on issues including intellectual property, tariffs, kids online safety, competition, and domestic semiconductor manufacturing. It engaged on bills that seek to put the onus on app stores to verify users’ ages, for example. It’s the first quarter in which Apple has reported spending more than $3 million on lobbying. The disclosures show that leading AI companies are becoming increasingly active in policymaking, in a quarter that marks a lead-up to the midterm elections. OpenAI didn’t even spend $1 million on lobbying in a single quarter until this year, and didn’t spend more than half a million until the end of 2024. The most Anthropic spent in a single quarter last year was just over $1 million. And this quarter is the first in which Nvidia has spent more than $2 million. With issues like data center development and AI safety on many voters’ minds, AI lobbyists’ work will likely only increase no matter whichever party has control next year.

articles.title: AI agents are causing massive headaches for banks.
articles.summary:
According to Axios, banks have detected AI agents accessing customer accounts and taking actions, sometimes without clear authorization or instruction. JPMorgan, Citi, Bank of America, and Morgan Stanley have started to restrict or block some third-party access because of it. But more concerning, it seems the banks just don’t know what AI agents are doing or why:
> One bank executive told Axios they struggle to differentiate between agents, as well as whether an agent has been authorized by a user or has gone rogue and gained access to a customer account.

articles.title: Google’s AI overview led some people to think they were donating to James Talarico when they weren’t.
articles.summary:
Instead, their money went to a political action committee that funneled the money to the reelection campaign of Colorado’s Democratic Senator John Hickenlooper. According to The Atlantic:
> The mix-up wasn’t all AI’s fault. The link led to a misleading donation page that carried Talarico’s name and picture, and specified only at the bottom that the money would go to Hickenlooper. But Google’s AI tool evidently didn’t read the fine print. And perhaps no one would have clicked on it had Google not highlighted the page in an authoritative-sounding AI response.

articles.title: The disastrous PHP vulnerabilities were exploited days before the patch
articles.summary: A hacker attempted to exploit the PHP bug that impacted sites across the web four days before a patch was released, according to Amazon Threat Intelligence.
articles.body: Hackers attempted to exploit the PHP flaws impacting sites across the web days before they were patched, according to a report from Amazon Threat Intelligence. CJ Moses, Amazon chief information security officer, writes that the company’s security team found a PHP2Shell exploit attempt on October 17th through a monitoring system designed to bait hackers, as reported earlier by Wired and Bleeping Computer. On Wednesday, websites scrambled to apply a patch for two critical security vulnerabilities affecting PHP, a programming language used by a large portion of the internet, including WordPress sites. The flaws — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — could allow hackers to execute malicious code remotely on vulnerable devices. Elizabeth Barron, the PHP Foundation’s executive director, tells The Verge that “to our knowledge, there has been no successful attempt at remote code execution” but stresses that updating affected systems is “imperative.” The PHP Foundation initially theorized the bug in 2024, and while its security team came up with potential solutions, a fix was delayed due to “backward compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service potential, or requiring changes to many third-party extensions which seemed impossible to coordinate.” As the PHP Foundation prepared to ship the fix this week, details about the bugs began trickling out on forums and social media, with some security firms releasing information about them before the official release. But the report from Amazon Threat Intelligence suggests a bad actor may have identified the vulnerability before details started leaking. “While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” Moses writes. Amazon Threat Intelligence discovered several other exploitation attempts on October 21st in the hours before the patch’s release. “We are confident that a serious vulnerability with a fix stuck on hard trade-offs would now reach the PHP Foundation leadership much sooner, as we’re changing processes so leadership can help steer the situation to a timely resolution,” the PHP Foundation says. “We are now prioritizing measures to make sure vulnerabilities that need similarly complex fixes get resolved faster when they are reported in the future.”

articles.title: ‘Behemoth’ El Niño could be ‘off the charts,’ forecasters warn
articles.summary: Its strength may be “off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades.”
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Meteorologists are continuing to warn of the El Niño weather event expected to impact us throughout the winter, with a new climate outlook from the World Meteorological Organization suggesting it “could be unprecedented in strength.”

In an update Wednesday, the WMO said this year’s El Niño weather pattern could be so strong, it could “literally [be] off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades.”

A main focus of forecasting El Niño comes down to sea surface temperatures. In the Pacific, an “anomaly of 0.5 [degrees Celsius] above normal” can trigger an El Niño alert from the WMO, according to the United Nations. Between next month and January, WMO has forecast temperatures could rise 3.8 degrees Celsius above average.

“This El Niño is a behemoth,” the UN’s emergency relief chief, Tom Fletcher, said Wednesday , further describing it as “a wrecking ball,” packed with “extreme heat, droughts, and floods.” Its effects are expected to “be felt long after” it peaks at the end of 2026, WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said during a press conference, echoing other recent forecasts .

This strong, long-lasting El Niño is expected to have a “pretty substantial impact” on the weather we see over the next several months, Brian James, Nexstar chief meteorologist, previously said.

As we head into winter, how El Niño plays out will be very different for the northern half of the country and the southern half . Broadly speaking, the northern states will be drier and warmer than normal, while southern states will be cooler and wetter. Recent seasonal outlooks follow that pattern.

“Based on what I am seeing now, I am officially concerned,” Daniel Swain, a prominent climate scientist at the California Institute for Water Resources, said on social media recently, as reported by Nexstar’s KTLA. “We’ve never seen an event this big before in the context of our rapidly warming climate … The warning lights are flashing.”

Chances high for El Niño to be ‘historic event’

Earlier this month, NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center said El Niño “strengthened further” in September, with “a strong-to-very strong El Niño likely” from January through March.

“Chances remain high for a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950,” the CPC explained . “With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed.”

In late September, Columbia University climate scientist Azhar Ehsan, in a briefing to the media, provided a chart showing the probability of El Niño lasting until spring was “100% to 99%.”

“I wrote near-certain but it’s 100%,” he said at the time.

As it has been, NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center agrees El Niño is 100% sticking around for about six more months, though a La Niña pattern may not be too far away (denoted by the blue bar).

El Niño is on track to reach its peak in December, the WMO’s most recent Global Seasonal Climate Update showed. The report suggests sea-surface temperatures are only expected to “increase to record levels” between now and December, according to a press release .

“El Niño doesn’t add new heat to the planet. It releases heat the ocean has already been storing beneath the surface – which is why a strong event so often becomes one of the hottest years measured (as with 2024),” Saulo told the Global Heat Forum in Bangkok earlier this month. “The ocean it’s drawing from is the warmest we’ve ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release.”

Ehsan said in a September media briefing that this year’s atmospheric evolution looks similar to that of 1997 , when one of the strongest-ever El Niños formed. That winter was characterized by broken records and “unusual extremes,” climate researchers said in an April 1998 National Climatic Data Center report .

It was the U.S.’s second-warmest and seventh-wettest winter since 1895, and the super-strong El Niño contributed to chaotic weather from coast to coast : the Northeast was hit with ice storms, the Southeast and California were drenched with flooding, deadly tornadoes tore across Florida. There were weeks of storminess, and some cities went days without seeing the sun.

As daunting as it sounds, there may be some upsides to the El Niño . KTLA meteorologist Henry DiCarlo said earlier this week that the potential for higher-than-average seasonal rain could help combat the drought conditions California has been battling as of late .

Saulo, however, has warned that regions of the world could face severe drought, flooding, and increased heat.

“We cannot stop El Niño,” she said. “But we can prevent many of its worst human consequences.”

articles.title: Hegseth’s team broke WWII-era globe from Eisenhower’s office
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s team dropped and damaged a historic World War II-era globe previously used by Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower, a source familiar with the incident told The Hill on Thursday. While moving the artifact to the secretary’s office, Hegseth’s staff lost control of the 30-inch floor globe, causing it to crash on its…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s team dropped and damaged a historic World War II-era globe previously used by Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower, a source familiar with the incident told The Hill on Thursday.

While moving the artifact to the secretary’s office, Hegseth’s staff lost control of the 30-inch floor globe, causing it to crash on its base and resulting in an inches-wide gash near Antarctica, The Washington Post first reported Thursday .

The Post obtained images of the globe that showed the damage caused during the early February relocation attempt.

The Army’s press office referred The Hill to Hegseth’s office.

A Pentagon official confirmed to The Hill on Thursday the accident occurred while staff was transporting the replica of the Eisenhower globe as part of its relocation.

“Accidents happen, we are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired,” the official said in a statement. “It is unsurprising that the Washington Post is once again dedicating time to another inconsequential non-story.”

One of the Eisenhower globes has pen lines and markings from World War II on it, the source familiar told The Hill, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Early this year, Hegseth wanted the globe to be relocated to his office, but instead of trained curators, his staff dispatched its own team to do the job, the Post reported.

The Army office in possession of the artifact initially expected to consult with experts to make sure it could be safely transported, the newspaper reported.

Those plans were later interrupted when staffers were furloughed during a partial government shutdown as a result of a disagreement in Congress over the Trump administration’s immigration policy. After failing to reach the experts, Hegseth’s staff took the matter into its own hands, according to the Post.

The Army’s press office referred questions to the Pentagon.

It is unclear whether Hegseth personally asked for the globe to be moved to his office.

In recent years, another globe, which is around 40 inches in diameter and stands about 4 feet off the ground and is also connected to Eisenhower, was moved from the Army Center of Military History in Anniston, Ala., which is part of the Army Transformation and Training Command, to an Army base.

“When packing an asset of this size, we had to consider the context of its worth on many levels,” Craters & Freighters wrote in late December 2022. “Since the globe is considered priceless, we knew its value was much greater than financial, and that our team was heavily relied upon for a safe delivery.”

During World War II, Eisenhower led the attack on Nazi-occupied Europe as supreme commander of the Allied forces, including the D-Day landings in 1944, leading to the liberation of Paris. He later became the 34th U.S. President, serving from 1953 to 1961.

articles.title: Workers hit hard by rising employer health insurance costs
articles.summary: Costs are spiking for the millions of Americans who rely on workplace-sponsored health insurance, according to a survey released Thursday, with small businesses and their employees being hit especially hard. The average cost of a family plan increased by 5 percent, topping $28,000 this year, according to the annual Employer Health Benefits Survey from KFF.…
articles.body:
Costs are spiking for the millions of Americans who rely on workplace-sponsored health insurance, according to a survey released Thursday, with small businesses and their employees being hit especially hard.

The average cost of a family plan increased by 5 percent, topping $28,000 this year, according to the annual Employer Health Benefits Survey from KFF. Employers cover a lot of that, but the share that comes from workers’ paychecks is increasing.

Workers are paying $7,471 annually toward the premiums for employer-sponsored family health benefits this year on average, $621 more than in 2025 — a 9 percent increase.

Overall, the average deductible for U.S. workers is approaching $2,000 before insurance kicks in, according to the survey.

The increase hits particularly hard for employees at small firms with fewer than 200 workers. On average, those employees contributed $9,687 annually toward family coverage this year. That’s $2,847 more than workers in firms with at least 200 workers.

In 2025, smaller business employees paid roughly $8,900, compared with about $6,200 for larger companies, the report said.

Health cost worries have resonated throughout campaigns for the midterm elections, and Democrats have made those concerns a centerpiece of their messaging.

A recent KFF poll found healthcare costs, alongside gas prices, outranked food, housing and utilities as the top economic concern for voters in the midterm elections.

Employer-based healthcare is the dominant form of coverage in the country for people younger than 65 years. About 160 million Americans get health insurance through an employer.

The reasons for the spike vary. Higher prices for hospitals and other care are a significant driver of spending by insurers and employers, as is increased utilization of expensive prescription drugs, like GLP-1s for weight loss.

“We have been hearing a lot about Affordable Care Act and Medicaid cuts. Now add a 9% increase in what workers with employer coverage paid toward family premiums in 2026 to the reasons voters are so concerned about their health care costs,” KFF President and CEO Drew Altman said in a statement.

Last year, job-based premiums for a family of four averaged about $27,000. But the cost pressures don’t stop at premiums.

As provider prices rise, employer health plans and insurers have historically responded by shifting costs to workers and families through higher deductibles and other strategies that discourage care, like cutting coverage of GLP-1 drugs and aggressive prior authorization. Companies are also increasingly restricting employees’ choices of doctors or hospitals.

KFF’s annual health benefits survey of large and small employers includes roughly 1,900 employers with 10 or more workers.

articles.title: Pentagon advances some wind projects after freeze
articles.summary: The Trump administration is advancing some wind projects after a court order required it to do so. A White House official said Thursday that an initial set of wind projects under Pentagon review have been released. The official said this represents two projects located in Maine and South Dakota. The official said the Defense Department…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is advancing some wind projects after a court order required it to do so.

A White House official said Thursday that an initial set of wind projects under Pentagon review have been released. The official said this represents two projects located in Maine and South Dakota.

The official said the Defense Department will keep evaluating wind projects on a case-by-case basis.

The official also described the move as clearing the path for a bipartisan energy bill in the Senate. That legislation — which is expected to cut down on barriers, including environmental laws for energy projects — is the result of a tenuous deal between Democrats and Republicans, and comes after significant ire from the left over the Trump administration’s moves to hold up renewable energy projects.

The advancement of the two projects comes after the administration earlier this year froze approvals for onshore wind projects, citing potential interference with doppler radars. A lawsuit earlier this year said at least 125 utility-scale projects in 25 states were impacted.

In August, a federal judge halted the Pentagon’s freeze as a case against it plays out. Earlier this week, organizations that sued over the department’s treatment of wind projects asked the court to take additional steps to enforce the order, saying the administration was failing to comply with it.

The move also comes as the Trump administration has taken other steps to hamper wind energy in recent weeks. It recently requested to reconsider previously approved permits for several offshore wind projects.

Sen. Martin Heinrich (N.M.), a key Democratic negotiator on the energy bill, called on the Trump administration to do more to unlock the projects it has stalled.

“Approving the routine upgrades in these two projects is obviously welcome, but there are hundreds of onshore wind projects in limbo that I’d like to see moving also, to get much needed gigawatts onto the grid,” Heinrich said in a statement shared with The Hill.

“I am optimistic that the White House appreciates the importance of good faith, forward momentum on these permits. And I look forward to seeing more move forward in the coming weeks,” he added.

articles.title: Data broker opt-out: How retirees can protect their data
articles.summary: A Minnesota murder suspect's notebook listed 11 people search websites, raising urgent questions about data broker opt-out and online privacy risks.
articles.body: Your home address, phone number and relatives' names may be sitting on people search websites you've never visited. Anyone who finds those listings could learn more about you than you're comfortable sharing. A data broker opt-out can help reduce that exposure, especially during retirement, when protecting your finances, family and home becomes a priority. And a tragic case in Minnesota shows why publicly available personal information deserves a closer look. Here's what happened in Minnesota and the steps you can take to make your personal information harder to find online. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You'll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET/8 AM PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME Minnesota attacks expose a troubling privacy risk In June 2025, Minnesota lawmaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark, were murdered in a targeted attack. State Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, were seriously injured in a separate shooting. Investigators discovered notebooks containing the names of public officials and a handwritten list of 11 people search websites in the suspect's vehicle. The list included TruePeopleSearch, Spokeo, Pipl, PeopleFinders, BeenVerified, Whitepages, TruthFinder, Intelius, Ownerly, USSearch and PeopleLooker. The notes described which services were free and what information someone could find through them. However, the discovery alone did not establish whether the websites supplied the victims' addresses. On June 11, Vance Boelter pleaded guilty to federal charges in the murders, shootings and stalking of the victims. He was sentenced July 23 to two consecutive life terms, plus 40 years, in federal prison. Separate state charges remain pending. The case raised an unsettling question: How easily could someone find your home address and information about your family? What data brokers know about you Data brokers collect information from public records, online activity, commercial databases and other sources. They then combine those details into profiles that businesses and individuals may be able to purchase or access. Some companies specialize in marketing information. Others operate people search websites that make personal details available through free searches or paid reports. Depending on the company and the available records, those profiles may include: Not every broker collects or sells all this information. Credit reporting agencies also operate under different legal requirements than many people search services. Still, these records can reveal details you never intended to share with strangers. For a closer look at how criminals assemble this information, read our CyberGuy report on how scammers build a profile on you using data brokers. Want to see how much of your personal information may already be exposed? Get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web: Cyberguy.com Why exposed personal information is risky for retirees Scammers can use publicly available details to make their stories more convincing. As a result, a suspicious call or message may sound surprisingly personal. Here are some of the potential risks. Even if you've never experienced one of these problems, reducing the amount of personal information available online can make it harder for someone to research you. THE SECRET LIST THAT TELLS SCAMMERS YOU'RE AN EASY TARGET How to opt out of data brokers yourself You can request removal from many people search websites for free. However, each company may have different requirements, and removing a listing doesn't always prevent it from returning. Here's how to get started. A new privacy shortcut for California residents If you live in California, you now have another option. The state's free Delete Request and Opt-out Platform (DROP) at privacy.ca.gov/drop/ launched in January 2026. It allows eligible residents to submit one deletion request to more than 600 registered data brokers. Beginning August 1, 2026, covered data brokers were required to start processing those requests. The system also requires recurring checks for matching information, although legal exceptions apply and removal is not immediate. Other states have their own privacy laws and removal rights, so your options may depend on where you live. How a data removal service can help protect your personal information If manually contacting dozens of websites sounds exhausting, a data removal service can handle much of the work for you. These services help identify data brokers and people-search websites that may have your information. They can also submit removal requests on your behalf and follow up when necessary. Depending on the provider and subscription plan, available features may include: To get started, choose a reputable data removal service, create an account and provide the information needed to identify your records. You'll typically need to authorize the service to submit removal requests on your behalf. Some providers also offer family plans that cover multiple household members. Before subscribing, compare the websites each service covers, its removal process, ongoing monitoring features and subscription costs. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. What a data removal service cannot do Even with automated removal, some personal information may remain publicly accessible. Property ownership records, government databases and certain court records can continue displaying details about you. Data removal services generally cannot force government agencies to delete legally available public records. Additionally, not every website must honor a removal request. Some services offer custom removals, but legal restrictions and technical limitations can prevent certain information from being deleted. Removing data broker listings also cannot undo previous data breaches or guarantee that scammers will stop contacting you. Still, reducing the number of websites exposing your information can make it harder for strangers to find personal details. For retirees, that added privacy can help reduce exposure to targeted scams and unwanted contact. Kurt's key takeaways What concerns me most is how much someone can learn about you without ever meeting you. Your address, family connections and personal history can give scammers information they can use to gain your trust. And once that information starts circulating, controlling where it goes becomes difficult. That's why I recommend taking a proactive approach. Start by finding out what's publicly available, remove what you can and keep checking. If the process becomes overwhelming, a reputable data removal service can help with the ongoing work. You may never erase every trace of yourself from the internet, but you can make your personal information harder to find. articles.title: Talarico accuses Musk of buying his ‘own personal U.S. Senator’
articles.summary: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico hit back at Elon Musk, accusing the technology mogul of trying to “buy his own personal” senator through massive campaign donations for Talarico’s opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). “There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator,”…
articles.body:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico hit back at Elon Musk, accusing the technology mogul of trying to “buy his own personal” senator through massive campaign donations for Talarico’s opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton (R).

“There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator,” Talarico wrote Wednesday on social platform X , the social media platform owned by Musk.

Talarico was responding to a recent post from Musk, who suggested “there is something deeply wrong” with the Democratic nominee. Musk formally endorsed Paxton earlier this week after campaign finance records indicated the SpaceX CEO spent more than $150 million on his candidacy.

“The fate of Texas and America is at stake. Vote for @KenPaxtonTX today,” Musk wrote Tuesday.

Federal election filings released last week showed Musk was the single donor to Texas PAC — a political action committee backing Paxton’s run — in the third quarter. Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, which transferred the funds to Texas PAC shortly after.

Paxton and Talarico are in a dead heat, according to a new poll from Emerson College Polling and The Hill, which showed Talarico with 48 percent support and Paxton with 46 percent.

Musk has various ties to Texas, managing several business ventures in the Lone Star State.

Starbase, the SpaceX industrial complex, is located in Texas and became an incorporated city last year. Musk’s tunnel company, The Boring Company, is based in San Antonio, and he is also developing a semiconductor and AI compute facility in Grimes County, Texas.

Despite previously saying he would pull back his political involvement, Musk is the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterms.

articles.title: Republican politicians have embraced anti-Indian racism — and it’s costing them votes
articles.summary: Some Indian American conservatives say bigotry against their community has driven them away from the party they once supported.﻿
articles.body: Two years ago, University of Houston student Vasant Bhatt was doing everything he could to help Republicans regain power. He knocked doors for Sen. Ted Cruz’s reelection campaign and helped organize his community for Donald Trump, two victories he, like many other Republicans, celebrated in 2024. But this week, Bhatt did something unexpected: He voted for Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, and he publicly urged others to do the same. Bhatt, whose father is a small-business owner, tells The Verge he was initially drawn to the Republican Party due to its economic principles. “The strong belief in individual liberty and limited government,” he says, led him to identify as a conservative. More recently, however, another aspect of his family’s experience has driven him away from the party. As an Indian American, Bhatt feels increasingly unwelcome in a party where racist rhetoric is becoming far too common. [Media: “There’s isolated individuals, but I think there’s an ecosystem as well,” Bhatt says. He has gotten used to people telling him to go back to India, but recently, he’s noticed anti-Indian racism increasing in both frequency and intensity. He wasn’t surprised when prominent conservative commentators replied to his post implying he’s not a real American. The X account for the Waco Young Republicans accused him of voting “entirely based on his loyalty to a foreign people over Americans.” Indian Americans are reliable voters, with about 70 percent of the voting-eligible population showing up to the polls in presidential election years. And there were signs that the electorate was moving to the right, albeit only slightly: The percentage of Indian American voters who lean Democrat dropped from 59 percent in 2020 to 55 percent four years later. About one-third of Indian Americans supported Trump in 2024 — by no means a majority, but still a sign their votes were up for grabs. Since then, however, they’ve become a favored target for racist self-proclaimed “heritage Americans.” Both fringe and mainstream conservatives have portrayed Indian Americans as stealing high-paying tech jobs from white workers and undermining American unity. Conservative commentator Chris Rufo — who rose to prominence by agitating against diversity efforts in public schools — even posted a video dissecting the so-called “Indian Question” in which he concluded that it’s “natural” for people to want to stick to their own kind. The right’s embrace of anti-Indian racism is now threatening to reverse Republicans’ recent gains with Indian American voters while promoting immigration restrictions that could shape the country for years to come. Bhatt began to notice the shift shortly after Trump’s 2024 victory but says it has become especially intense in the run-up to the midterm elections. In September, Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner, posted a picture of hundreds of University of Texas fans celebrating a football victory. “The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined,” French wrote, referring to the fact that many students in the foreground appeared to be of South Asian descent. Some Texas Republicans condemned French’s racism, but French stood by his comments, and others have defended him. “Watching people like Jack Posobiec rationalize, excuse, minimize, and even prop up this rhetoric by defending folks like Bo French, I’m not really surprised,” says Bhatt. [Media: A few weeks after French’s comments, Vice President JD Vance used his announcement that the Trump administration would be reducing some tech companies’ ability to hire foreign employees as an opportunity to call workers on H-1B visas “foreign indentured servants.” India’s Ministry of External Affairs called Vance’s comments “deeply offensive.” Anti-Indian rhetoric has also translated into policy change. The Washington Post notes that Republican politicians became more willing to engage in attacks on legal immigrants — including Indian Americans — after Trump’s immigration crackdown led to a drastic decrease in unauthorized border crossings. Now that Trump appears to have “solved” the problem of illegal immigration by shutting down asylum at the border, and has unleashed ICE on immigrants living in the country, nativists have found a new target in H-1B workers, many of whom are Indian immigrants. Since returning to office, Trump has raised the price of H-1B visas to upwards of $100,000 and waged a silent war on legal immigration, not only slashing the number of people who could legally come to the US but also sending naturalization rates plummeting. Spokespeople for ICE and the Department of Homeland Security now promote the idea of “remigration,” or forcibly returning immigrants to their countries of origin regardless of their legal status. The White House has even celebrated the fact that legal immigration has fallen since Trump’s return to office. These policies are animated by a belief, prevalent among a faction of Republicans led by White House adviser Stephen Miller, that the problem with immigration isn’t whether people come to America legally, but what types of people come here. A growing chorus of “heritage Americans” see all non-white immigrants as incapable of assimilating to American culture, and they’ve selected Indians as their primary target. “I spent years within conservative politics, and I realized that my convictions don’t mean anything if I’m not going to be regarded as an American, or if I’m going to be regarded as a second-class citizen,” says Bhatt. Signs of the Republican Party’s anti-Indian turn have been percolating for years. Shortly after Trump selected Vance as his running mate, far-right streamer Nick Fuentes declared a “groyper war” on the Trump-Vance campaign. Fuentes, who is Mexican American, claimed that Vance’s marriage to an Indian American woman meant he “doesn’t value his racial identity.” In response, Vance denounced Fuentes, calling him a “white supremacist” — but that was all before the election. Trump’s 2024 inroads among voters of color, including Indian Americans, shocked pundits who expected that his nativist rhetoric and policies would drive Black, Latino, and Asian voters toward the Democratic Party. Former White House adviser Steve Bannon even claimed MAGA had become a multiracial, working-class coalition — and he wasn’t entirely wrong. But in late 2024, as the GOP should have been taking a victory lap, two factions of the MAGA movement clashed over H-1B visas. The debate scrambled political alliances, with Elon Musk — a promoter of the racist “great replacement” conspiracy theory — arguing that foreign-born workers are essential to American innovation. Though Musk is an immigrant himself, his comments received far less vitriol than those made by former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who said H-1Bs are needed in part because American culture “has venerated mediocrity over excellence for way too long.” Critics pointed to Ramaswamy’s comments as proof that Indian Americans — even those who, like him, were born in the United States — are incapable of assimilating. On X, Ramaswamy’s opponents said that his comments were indicative of “thinly veiled ethnic resentment” and doubled down on their claims that the primary function of H-1B visas is to replace American workers. Despite Musk’s position on visas, it should come as no surprise that X has helped push anti-Indian rhetoric from the fringes to the forefront of conservative politics. Conversations that wouldn’t seem out of place on 4chan or The Daily Stormer are now happening on a mainstream social media site with millions of users. “It really started after Elon’s takeover of Twitter, and it went into full overdrive mode after the ’24 election, in November, when Vivek joined DOGE,” says Anang Mittal, a longtime conservative strategist who previously worked for Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY). “That was the beginning of, ‘Okay, it’s open season on out-and-out racism.’” Mittal suspects that Republican politicians feel like they can entertain anti-Indian racism without losing much support among voters, in part because Indian Americans are such a small slice of the population. An estimated 5.2 million Indian Americans live in the United States, constituting just over 1.5 percent of the total US population. “They decided there’s no price to be paid when it comes to engaging in language that treats Indian immigrants as outsiders and not compatible with American culture,” says Mittal. Republicans’ increasingly explicit anti-Indian sentiment may help cost them in the midterms. A February survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace found that seven in 10 Indian Americans disapprove of Trump’s second-term performance — but it also shows that Democrats have lost support among Indian Americans since 2020, and just 46 percent identify as Democrats today. These remarks have had real-world consequences far beyond the realm of electoral politics: Last week, authorities arrested a 19-year-old man who allegedly attempted a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois. Law enforcement reportedly seized weapons, ammunition, Nazi paraphernalia, and a gas canister with an anti-South Asian slur written on it, as well as a manifesto in which the alleged shooter fantasized about killing non-white people. The alleged shooter’s manifesto echoed “a lot of the narratives that you see online,” says Bhatt. “When you spend months watching people make generalizations about your community, and question your loyalties, and somehow make the presumption that our presence in America is undesirable, you are painting a target on people’s back.”

articles.title: Delaware senator calls on NFL to explain handling of Jalen Hurts health issue
articles.summary: Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) is demanding answers from the NFL on how the Philadelphia Eagles handled quarterback Jalen Hurts’s blood clotting issue, which led to the end of his season last week. In a letter to the NFL this week, Rochester said Hurts’s issue “is deeply personal to me,” explaining “my late husband and…
articles.body:
Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) is demanding answers from the NFL on how the Philadelphia Eagles handled quarterback Jalen Hurts’s blood clotting issue , which led to the end of his season last week.

In a letter to the NFL this week, Rochester said Hurts’s issue “is deeply personal to me,” explaining “my late husband and the love of my life, Charles Rochester, tore his Achilles tendon playing a game of pickup basketball before a business meeting. Blood clots traveled to his heart and lungs and, at the age of 52, he died.”

“As I understand it, Jalen Hurts was cleated in the calf during the Eagles’ Week 4 loss to the Rams. After flying to London for a game against the Jaguars, an ultrasound found a superficial blood clot in his calf. Conflicting reports suggest Mr. Hurts was hospitalized and advised to stay awake until kickoff as a safety precaution. He played, but a follow-up ultrasound days later found the clot had moved. Further testing ultimately revealed the clot had spread to both of his lungs,” the lawmaker wrote.

The Democrat, an Eagles fan, said she was “deeply relieved that Mr. Hurts’s story did not end the way my husband’s did,” estimating clots affect more than 900,000 people in the United States each year. She wrote, “The NFL’s influence and reach offer a vital opportunity to turn this tragedy into a force for preventing lost lives both in sports and outside of it.”

The Eagles announced Hurts would be shut down for the season as a result of the clotting issue, which was discovered before he was allowed to play against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London and travel back to the United States with his team.

Eagles coach Nick Sirianni deflected questions about how Hurts’s injury was handled, telling reporters earlier this week, “I lean on our guys in all those situations. I’m a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them. It’s not just me that has major care for our players. It’s them as well.”

The NFL Players Association has called for an independent investigation into the Hurts saga, which NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he welcomes after a league official told The Athletic it was aware of no wrongdoing by the Eagles as it treated Hurts.

articles.title: The FCC is beginning to block gadgets with ‘foreign surveillance chips’
articles.summary: The FCC has used its new power to block gadgets with computer chips if the chip’s maker is on a banned list.
articles.body: On October 13th, Brendan Carr’s FCC gave itself a new power — it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security. Today, it’s exercising that power for the first time, blocking two gadgets because they contain “foreign surveillance chips,” the FCC claims. The agency doesn’t say which specific gadgets it blocked, and it didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment, but it does name the “surveillance chip”: it’s a HiVision Hi3516CV610 UHD Smart Vision SoC, a chip that turns a raw camera sensor into a home security camera, a dashcam, or the like. It’s often sold as a package with a Sony camera sensor and sometimes even a lens already on board, according to listings we viewed on AliExpress. The FCC is calling it a foreign surveillance chip because HiVision advertises it as “designed for the surveillance market” with “[b]uilt in detection algorithms for human faces,” the FCC explains — and because HiVision is a subsidiary of Huawei, one of the first telecom companies the US government decided to call a national security risk. Huawei is indeed on the FCC’s Covered List, and the FCC’s new power helps it close a loophole where companies could sneak in banned companies’ products inside another company’s gadgets. It did something similar when it gave itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets, and when it gave itself the power to block modular radio transmitters. As with the router ban and the Roomba ban, he question remains: is the FCC keeping people safer, or just picking winners and losers while making a show of enforcement? We’ve asked the agency many times to chat about its efforts, but it won’t engage.

articles.title: Hegseth bars US forces from using undisclosed information to bet on Polymarket, Kalshi
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth barred all Pentagon staff from using undisclosed information to place wagers on forthcoming U.S. military action using betting platforms and prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. “Make no mistake why this matters. Our enemies watch movements in these markets,” Hegseth said in a memo, first obtained by CBS News. “When an American…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth barred all Pentagon staff from using undisclosed information to place wagers on forthcoming U.S. military action using betting platforms and prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket.

“Make no mistake why this matters. Our enemies watch movements in these markets,” Hegseth said in a memo , first obtained by CBS News . “When an American Service member, intelligence professional, or other Department civilian engages in a financial transaction on a military outcome, they create a signal.”

One Pentagon official confirmed the authenticity of the memo to The Hill on Thursday.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Prediction market platforms exploded in popularity this year, raising concerns in Washington over the potential for insider trading by government officials. National security experts have warned bad actors can leverage the markets to identify upcoming operations.

Hegseth warned those signals can be aggregated and exploited by “hostile” foreign intelligence services to anticipate U.S. military movements, timing and targeting.

“The lives of our Service members often depend on the enemy not knowing what is coming,” the Defense secretary said in the memo dated Tuesday. “The men and women who carry our flag into harm’s way deserve a Force that protects them – not one that exposes them to the enemy for personal gain.”

Hegseth said violations could result in administrative, disciplinary and “where appropriate, criminal action” under the Uniform Code of Military Justice “and/or applicable federal law.”

The memo comes nearly six months after a U.S. soldier was arrested for allegedly using classified information to place a prediction market bet on the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

Prosecutors said Army soldier Gannon Ken Van Dyke was involved in the planning of the Maduro operation in January and placed about $33,000 worth of bets prior to the incident.

Van Dyke entered a not guilty plea in late April.

The arrest of Van Dyke was the first high-profile case around alleged insider trading on events contracts, prompting a flurry of bills on Capitol Hill to bar elected officials or federal employees from participating in prediction markets.

A White House teleprompter operator was later placed on leave in July over allegedly making online bets on President Trump’s speeches. The operator, Gabriel Perez, was ordered to pay more than $172,000.

articles.title: Pentagon locks in 10-year F-35 jet deal
articles.summary: Lockheed Martin and the Pentagon have penned an initial deal to produce at least 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets over ‌the next 10 years, the Defense Department announced Thursday. As part of the agreement, Lockheed will put forward at least $7 billion in its own funding “for initiatives that support the F-35 program,” according…
articles.body:
Lockheed Martin and the Pentagon have penned an initial deal to produce at least 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets over ‌the next 10 years, the Defense Department announced Thursday.

As part of the agreement, Lockheed will put forward at least $7 billion in its own funding “for initiatives that support the F-35 program,” according to a Pentagon statement.

In a separate statement, Lockheed said it is looking to produce 156 aircraft a year under the deal.

The F-35, considered ​the world’s most advanced fighter jet, has been the subject of much congressional scrutiny due to the program’s cost overruns and the high price tag of each aircraft.

After he was first elected, then-President-elect Trump in 2017 pushed Lockheed to significantly lower the cost of each F-35, which the company agreed to.

Defense contractors have argued that under the typical way the U.S. government funds weapons procurement — in batches with funding needing to be secured every year through congressional appropriation — it makes it difficult to keep production lines running consistently.

Lockheed said the agreement eliminates “the annual contracting cycle that has historically strained the industrial base,” as it “will enable bulk procurement of raw materials and critical parts, slashing turnaround times and reducing logistics bottlenecks.”

The Pentagon didn’t reveal the potential total cost of the newly announced deal, which is labeled as a prearranged long-term contract and does not constitute an order. Execution of the agreement remains subject to congressional authorization and appropriations.

“If granted multiyear authority and associated appropriations in the coming months, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will work to finalize contract terms, pricing, and schedules through a formal contract award,” the company said.

Lockheed added that the deal is expected to save taxpayers billions of dollars over the F-35’s lifecycle and estimates it will support 317,000 U.S. jobs and generate nearly $79 ⁠billion in ​annual economic activity over the next decade.

“We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale,” Under Secretary of Defense Michael Duffey said in the department’s statement. “This agreement ⁠with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win.”

Under the deal, Lockheed would build the 850 fighter jets, cover international orders and produce initial spare parts and modification kits.

images.caption: FILE – A Lockheed Martin F-16 Jet fighter performs its demonstration flight, June 22, 2011, at the 49th Paris Air Show at Le Bourget airport, east of Paris. People living in and around Washington D.C. experienced a rare, if startling, sound: A sonic boom. The U.S. military had dispatched a fighter jet on Sunday, June 4, 2023, to intercept an unresponsive business plane that was flying over restricted airspace. The Air Force gave the F-16 permission to fly faster than the speed of sound to catch up with it. (AP Photo/Francois Mori, File)
